USS Indianapolis. A heavy cruiser that sank on July 30, 1945, after delivering atomic bomb components to Tinian Island just days before the Hiroshima strike. Torpedoed by a Japanese submarine, she went down in twelve minutes, and of her 1,196 crew, only 316 survived the sinking and subsequent four days adrift. Her loss stands as one of the Navy's greatest peacetime disasters.

Indianapolis completed her secret mission delivering uranium and bomb components for the Little Boy atomic bomb to Tinian Island on July 26, 1945, just four days before Hiroshima. She was then torpedoed by Japanese submarine I-58 on July 30, 1945, at 00:14 hours and sank in twelve minutes, giving the crew minimal time to abandon ship. The sinking itself killed approximately 300 crew, but the remaining 900 spent four days in the ocean where shark attacks, dehydration, and exposure claimed 600 more, one of the highest casualty rates in naval history.

The disaster remained classified for years because of its connection to the atomic bomb, delaying rescue efforts and investigations. The ship's captain, Charles B. McVay III, was court-martialed in a controversial decision that haunted him for decades. He was exonerated posthumously in 2001. Her fate is immortalized in survivor accounts and memoirs, and her cargo had been instrumental in delivering to the Pacific Theater the weapon that would end the war. As one of the last American warships lost in the theater, her sinking marked the war's final tragedy.
